one_liner: Experimental Rust Python 3.14 interpreter with a Cranelift JIT; about 2x CPython 3.14.8 on its own fixtures.
what_it_does: A from-scratch Python interpreter in Rust (lexer, parser, compiler, VM, C-API layer) that aims to run unmodified CPython 3.14 code, including binary wheels through an emulated C-API, with a `weavepy` CLI that is argv-compatible with `python`. It is meant as a drop-in for the `python` executable, and the `weavepy` crate can also be embedded as a library. It is not on crates.io (version 0.0.0), so you build it from the workspace.
how_it_is_fast: Tiered execution: a bytecode interpreter with specialization and call-shape inline caches, a Cranelift-backed tier-2 JIT on by default (typed scalar, object, dict, string and slots lanes with guards and deopt back to exact interpreter frames, native-to-native calls, OSR at loop back edges), and since PR #83 a baseline 'frame compiler' for loops that tier 2 declines. Native Rust implementations replace pure-Python stdlib paths (deque, datetime, pickle, regex, map/filter), small ints and floats are unboxed, and tracebacks are built lazily. The biggest wins are integer and float loop kernels that compile entirely to native code.
when_to_use: CPU-bound pure-Python loops over ints and floats (sumvm, nested_loops, jitloop ran in 0.05-0.08 of CPython 3.14.8's time; spectral_norm 0.20; fib 0.36).
Experimenting with a faster CPython-compatible runtime on code that does not depend on CPython object identity or obscure C-API corners.
Research into tiered JITs for Python: the repo keeps RFCs, per-pass performance reports and raw census data, and a Cranelift tier-2 design you can read.
Workloads where per-process startup matters slightly: the parity run measured 19.4 ms vs CPython's 24.5 ms for the startup fixture (x86-64 host).
when_not_to_use: Class-heavy OO code like DeltaBlue: 3.03x CPython's time; class-attribute reads through an instance cost about 357 instructions vs CPython's 36, and isinstance about 1,635 vs 271.
Memory-constrained or import-heavy processes: after importing logging or asyncio, peak RSS is 2-2.5x CPython's, and imports retire 1.3-1.8x CPython's instructions.

Production use: single author, 3 stars, 0 open issues, no releases or crates.io package; performance moved from 2.75x slower than CPython (committed macOS-aarch64 baseline, early September) to 0.50x in four weeks of large PRs.
Code relying on CPython object identity of numbers: the unboxed numeric model makes test_marshal's id()-based new-object checks unsatisfiable (documented divergence).
Generator-heavy and dict-heavy code where it is at or behind parity (generators 1.10x, dict_ops 0.92-1.06x of CPython's time).

integration.form: built binary (Cargo workspace; the weavepy crate is embeddable but unpublished)
integration.dependencies: Rust toolchain; Cranelift 0.132 (JIT), rustls (ssl), rusqlite (sqlite3), vendored expat; tools/pgo_build.py needs the llvm-tools rustup component
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.93 (workspace rust-version, set by Cranelift 0.132); rust-toolchain.toml tracks stable
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS x86-64 and ARM64, Windows (CI lanes on all three); benchmarks only on macOS
integration.thread_safety: GIL by default with eval-breaker hand-off from JIT code; a free-threaded lane exists (PR #75) and PEP 684/734 sub-interpreters are supported
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: argv-compatible `python` replacement that the README says passes 546 of 550 CPython regrtest labels and 40 ecosystem rows (pandas, Django, FastAPI), but the parity report lists test_capi, test_genexps, test_tempfile and test_utf8_mode failing on the dev host, plus a documented id() divergence for numbers

gotchas: Harness flaw: the headline 0.50 geomean is not over 24 fixtures as the doc states. crates/weavepy-bench/src/report.rs drops the three census fixtures (deque_ops, datetime_ops, pickle_bench) from the CPython geomean, so 0.50 covers 21 fixtures. The 0.75 vs main uses all 24 (base_geomean has no filter). Over all 24 rows of the doc's table the CPython ratio is 0.53, derived from page data.
The geomean leans on three JIT loop kernels (sumvm, jitloop, nested_loops at 0.05-0.08). Without them the other rows give about 0.70-0.71 of CPython's time (derived from page data).

Fixtures discard bench(n)'s return value, and the gate never checks outputs. Per-iteration times (about 2 ns for sumvm's loop) are consistent with native loops, not dead-code elimination, but correctness rests on the separate test suites.

Each sample is one bench(n) call in a fresh process (5 samples plus 1 discarded warm-up), so JIT compile time is inside the timed region. CPython is whatever `python3.14` is on PATH. An earlier pass on an Intel macOS host used CPython 3.14.5 built with PGO, LTO and the tail-call interpreter; the parity doc does not say how 3.14.8 was built.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick PyPy for a mature JIT that is far faster on loops and stable today. Codon, mypyc and Cython compile typed subsets for larger gains but are not drop-in. WeavePy is only worth a look if you need CPython 3.14 semantics and C-API wheels in a JIT runtime and accept experimental status; the CPython tail-calling interpreter is the conservative 3-5% option.
verified_claims_summary: The project's own bench gate on one Intel Core i9-9980HK macOS laptop ran a release build of WeavePy (PR #83 does not mention PGO) interleaved with CPython 3.14.8 from PATH. Per-fixture medians gave 0.50 of CPython's time as a geometric mean over 21 fixtures (0.53 over all 24 table rows), from 0.05 on sumvm to 3.03 on deltablue. The Rust version and CPython build flags are not stated.
status_note: Very active (daily large PRs by one author, last commit 2026-10-05), dual MIT/Apache-2.0, unpublished 0.0.0 workspace. Its performance claims are four weeks old and swing fast between reports, so treat it as an experiment, not a dependency.
